title: I used AI in a mobile life sim — player feedback exposed where it stopped helping
author: SnooChipmunks1891
selftext:
I'm building Deep Life Simulator, a mobile life sim about careers, education, relationships, family and businesses. It is free on iOS and Android, with ads and optional purchases that include gameplay benefits.



AI tools have assisted me with coding and some visual and marketing assets. The part I find most useful is speeding up small implementation and iteration tasks; the part that still needs human judgment is deciding what players can actually understand and trust.



An earlier launch thread got a lot of attention, but the most useful comments were not about the feature list. Players said they could not find early paths such as education, or stopped when they hit freezes, lost progress, and confusing navigation. That changed how I think about using AI in promotion too: an attractive asset or a long feature list cannot replace showing a real first session and making the next action obvious.



I am now using the feedback as a constraint: explain the first meaningful decision, keep the opening focused, and only claim a fix after it has been verified in the downloadable build.



For people using AI in game development: where do you draw the line between fast iteration and the research or playtesting that prevents you from building the wrong thing?



iOS: [https://apps.apple.com/app/id6749675615](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6749675615)

Android: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.deeplife.simulator](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.deeplife.simulator)

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body:
# I used AI to write a response to an AI-looking post — the first draft exposed where it stopped helping

I asked an AI to help me reply to a post about using AI in a mobile life sim. It gave me something polished, balanced, and deeply committed to making sure nobody could accuse it of having a point.

The most useful feedback was not about the wording. It was that the post sounded like it had been assembled from the approved parts of a thoughtful Reddit post: a personal project, a modest AI disclosure, a lesson about player feedback, and a question designed to generate discussion.

That changed how I think about using AI in replies too: a convincing format can make a response look considered without making it say anything.

I am now using that feedback as a constraint: keep the familiar structure, add a pinch of self-awareness, and only claim a joke after it has been verified in the downloadable sarcasm.

For people using AI to write posts: where do you draw the line between sounding authentic and explaining, in four tidy paragraphs, why you don’t sound authentic?
